paper_title: RoTA-Bench: Evaluating 3D Spatial Reasoning through Interactive Projection Alignment

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Can vision-language models turn 2D observations into 3D understanding that supports precise action? This requires inferring object geometry, anticipating the effects of rotation, and refining actions through visual feedback. We introduce RoTA-Bench to evaluate these abilities through interactive 3D-to-2D projection alignment. Given a target silhouette, a model observes a rotated object and chooses successive rotations to recover the target projection within a limited action budget. Our automated pipeline constructs silhouette-preserving 3D objects from 2D icons and uses reversible initialization to guarantee solvability, yielding 674 tasks and a stratified 100-task test set. Empirically, we find that (i) a substantial human-model gap persists: GPT-5.6-Sol succeeds on only 17% of tasks, whereas 20 undergraduate participants collectively complete the test set four times with a 100% success rate; (ii) image-space and pose-space progress can diverge: at matched states, the model more often improves silhouette overlap while worsening pose alignment than humans (19.4% vs. 10.9%); and (iii) fine-grained control is sensitive to interaction history: removing it leaves 96.8% of the model's actions at a coarse 30-degree step size and sharply reduces observed task success. These findings highlight the challenge of converting visual evidence into precise 3D control, beyond recognizing or matching individual images.

sections.title:
1 Introduction
Psychological and cognitive-science research establishes spatial perception as a foundational domain of cognitive ability
(Carroll, 1993), essential for maintaining object constancy across viewpoints (Shepard & Metzler, 1971) and recovering
three-dimensional geometry from two-dimensional projections (Richards et al., 1987) through the mental representation,
manipulation, and inference of shape and orientation. As vision-language models are increasingly applied in visual
question answering, interactive agents, and embodied systems (Chen et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2026), agents in interactive
settings such as embodied exploration and geometry-aware navigation must translate spatial understanding into physical
actions (Zhu et al., 2025). However, current models continue to face challenges in reasoning about three-dimensional
positions, orientations, and spatial relationships (Ma et al., 2025). Therefore, addressing these challenges requires
evaluation tools that assess whether models can turn 2D observations into 3D understanding that supports precise
action.
sections.content: However, current visual and spatial benchmarks fall short of this requirement. Static benchmarks evaluate spatial reasoning through passive question answering on fixed images (Johnson et al., 2017; Hudson & Manning, 2019; Yue et al., 2024; Lu et al., 2024), lacking action execution and closed-loop feedback entirely. Conversely, existing interactive benchmarks spanning software interfaces, visual mazes, and sliding puzzles (Zhou et al., 2024; Xie et al., 2024; Rodriguez Salgado, 2026; Mayer et al., 2025) focus on high-level task planning, tool invocation, or spatial pathfinding 1 MAC-AutoML Figure 1. RoTA-Bench overview. The benchmark contains 674 canonical tasks, with 100 test tasks selected by stratified sampling over reference path lengths. In the T-shirt example, the solver chooses discrete rotations from visual observations and receives updated views until projection IoU reaches 0.90 or another stopping rule applies. The right panel shows task success rates and final IoU on the test set; full results are reported in Table 1. in complex environments. In these settings, task success largely depends on coding ability, reasoning, and planning, rather than perceiving three-dimensional orientation from visual cues and translating it into action. To bridge this gap, inspired by classical insights on inferring three-dimensional shape from two-dimensional projections and silhouettes (Richards et al., 1987), we ask whether vision-language models can turn 2D observations into 3D understanding that supports precise action. Therefore, we introduce RoTA-Bench, an automatically constructed benchmark of interactive 3D-to-2D projection alignment. Our pipeline constructs three-dimensional objects from two-dimensional icons, generates initial orientations through reversible rotations, and guarantees solvability automatically. Given target silhouette and visual observations of the rotated object, the model selects rotation from 24 discrete actions at each step, receives an updated observation at the next step, and iteratively refines alignment within limited action budget. The benchmark contains 674 tasks, with stratified 100-task test set. Through evaluations of nine vision-language models, two agent configurations, and 20 undergraduate participants, each completing consecutive 20-task block from the 100-task test set, we find: First, substantial humanmodel gap persists: GPT-5.6-Sol succeeds on only 17% of tasks, whereas all 400 human task runs succeed. Second, imagespace and pose-space progress can diverge: at matched states, GPT-5.6-Sol more often improves silhouette overlap while worsening pose alignment than humans (19.4% vs. 10.9%). Third, fine-grained control is sensitive to interaction history: removing it leaves 96.8% of the models actions at coarse 30 step size and sharply reduces observed task success.

2.1 Multimodal Large Language Models and Spatial Reasoning
Early vision-language models established contrastive image–text alignment (Radford et al., 2021), while subsequent
architectures bridged visual encoders with language models for open-ended generation (Alayrac et al., 2022; Li et al.,
2023) and visual instruction following (Liu et al., 2023), scaled further by frontier models for advanced visual reasoning
(OpenAI, 2026a; Anthropic, 2026b,a; DeepMind, 2026; Qwen Team, 2026). To capture 3D geometry, specialized
architectures incorporate explicit 3D representations (Hong et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2024), whereas spatial VLMs infuse
coordinate reference frames (Song et al., 2025), metric relations (Chen et al., 2024), 3D object orientations (Ma et al.,
2025), and physical spatial intelligence (Wu et al., 2026). Embodied and vision-language-action architectures further
connect visual reasoning to physical planning (Huang et al., 2023; Rivera et al., 2025) and robotic execution (Driess

Unlike explicit 3D approaches, we examine whether models can turn 2D observations into 3D understanding that supports precise action.

sections.title:
2.3 Interactive Benchmarks for Visual and Spatial Reasoning
Interactive benchmarks evaluate visual and spatial reasoning through multi-turn closed-loop interaction. In embod-
ied AI, interactive benchmarks and agent architectures evaluate spatial reasoning through embodied navigation, long-
horizon task execution, and scene exploration (Shridhar et al., 2020; Savva et al., 2019; Driess et al., 2023; Rana et al.,
2023; Wang et al., 2023; Zhu et al., 2025); however, they predominantly emphasize macroscopic agent locomotion and
high-level semantic planning. Across digital domains, benchmarks test 2D layout grounding and interface parsing for
web browsing and operating system control (Zhou et al., 2024; Koh et al., 2024; Xie et al., 2024), yet they operate
strictly within 2D planar graphical displays. Closer to geometric reasoning, interactive benchmarks evaluate spatial

In contrast, RoTA-Bench evaluates whether models can turn 2D observations into 3D understanding that supports precise action through closed-loop projection alignment.

sections.title:
3.1 Motivation and Design Rationale
Classical studies in cognitive vision and psychology demonstrate that underlying 3D geometry and orientations can be
inferred from 2D visual contours (Richards et al., 1987) and compared through mental rotation (Shepard & Metzler,
1971). Inspired by these foundational insights, we formulate 3D orientation alignment as a projection-matching task:
rotating a 3D object until its 2D silhouette matches a target image. Restricting physical interaction to 3D rotation
provides two key methodological advantages. First, out-of-plane rotations induce nonlinear silhouette deformations,
aspect changes, and self-occlusion, creating an inherently visual challenge that resists textual representation. Second,
pure rotation cleanly decouples spatial orientation reasoning from extraneous physical dynamics—such as translational
drift, grasp affordances, and contact friction—allowing us to examine whether models can turn 2D observations into
3D understanding that supports precise action.
sections.content: To reduce reliance on semantic shortcuts and encourage visual-spatial reasoning, RoTA-Bench synthesizes 3D objects from 2D vector icons rather than drawing directly from common 3D CAD repositories, where familiar shapes may trigger pre-trained priors. By extruding 2D icons within spherical volume, this automated generation produces abstract, novel 3D geometries while mathematically guaranteeing that the canonical front view reproduces the original icon, preserving its fine-grained details (Appendix E). Finally, generating initial poses via sequences of reversible discrete rotations guarantees by construction that every task is solvable.

3.3 Dataset Construction
Our automated pipeline constructs the benchmark across three sequential phases: task generation, reference search, and
dataset construction, as summarized in Figure 2.

5.4 Action Association with Projection and Pose Discrepancies
We next examine whether rotation-angle choices rely more on visible projection overlap or on the underlying 3D pose
discrepancy. Figure 4 and Appendix Table 10 report their correlations with pre-action IoU and pose error. For GPT-5.6-
sections.content: 8 MAC-AutoML Sol, the correlation is stronger with IoU than with pose error (ρ = 0.536, 95% CI [0.617, 0.443] vs. ρ = 0.368, 95% CI [0.166, 0.532]). Human angles are strongly associated with both (ρ = 0.696, 95% CI [0.763, 0.633], and ρ = 0.751, 95% CI [0.675, 0.828]). Most evaluated models show the same relative pattern as GPT-5.6-Sol. These results suggest that most models rely more on projection overlap when choosing rotation angles, whereas humans use both projection overlap and 3D pose discrepancy. To conduct comparative analysis under the same conditions as closely as possible, we examine action consequences across the 211 exact state pairs shared by Human and GPT-5.6-Sol, where direct visual coverage before the matched actions is close (42.01% vs. 46.21%, Figure 5 and Appendix Table 8). We find that image-space and pose-space progress can diverge even when actions start from the same pose. Humans execute substantially more DC actions (33.18% vs. 23.70%), showing willingness to accept transient drops in 2D overlap to reduce underlying 3D pose error. Conversely, GPT-5.6-Sol executes nearly twice as many UF actions as humans (19.43% vs. 10.90%), showing greater willingness to accept increases in 3D pose error to improve 2D overlap. For the remaining outcomes, humans achieve far higher UC actions (50.24% vs. 34.60%) and avoid DF moves (5.69% vs. 22.27%). Together, these results show that image-space and pose-space progress can diverge: at matched states, GPT-5.6-Sol more often improves silhouette overlap while worsening pose alignment than humans.

sections.title:
6 Conclusion
RoTA-Bench evaluates whether vision-language models can turn 2D observations into 3D understanding that supports
precise action through interactive projection alignment. Its automated pipeline constructs silhouette-preserving 3D
objects and uses reversible initialization to guarantee solvability, yielding 674 tasks and a stratified 100-task test set.
Evaluations reveal a substantial human–model success gap, show that image-space and pose-space progress can diverge,
and find that fine-grained control is sensitive to interaction history. These findings highlight the challenge of converting
visual evidence into precise 3D control.

Ethics Statement All human evaluation experiments were conducted in accordance with ethical research standards, with informed consent obtained from all 20 undergraduate participants prior to the study. sections.content: K.1 Success Counts and Confidence Intervals Table 11 reports success counts and 95% Wilson confidence intervals for the nine models and two agents on the 100-task test set. These intervals summarize uncertainty under binomial task model. GPT-5.6-Sol has the highest observed success rate, but this ranking alone does not establish reliable difference between methods. Such comparisons require paired analysis on the same tasks. K.2 Response Formats and Episode Outcomes We audit the saved trajectories of all nine models and two agents on the 100 test tasks each. Table 12 reports episode outcomes and repeated actions. Stagnation denotes termination after consecutive rotations without suﬀicient improvement in the best IoU. STOP denotes an explicit stop below the success threshold, and Limit denotes termination at the step limit.
